title: What Is GMB Optimization? A Plain-English Guide to Google Business Profile
seo_title: What Is GMB Optimization? A Plain-English Guide
meta_description: What is GMB optimization? A plain-English look at improving your Google Business Profile, what Google says affects local rankings, and what to avoid.
excerpt: GMB optimization means making your Google Business Profile complete, accurate, and active. Here's what that involves, what Google says affects local visibility, and what you can do yourself.
tags: Google Business Profile, GMB, local SEO, Google Maps, reviews
topic: Plain-English explainer of Google Business Profile (GMB) optimization and a do-it-yourself checklist
reason: Informational entry point for the GMB optimization service page; captures people searching what GMB optimization is
body_html:
What is GMB optimization? It's the work of making your Google Business Profile, formerly Google My Business (GMB), complete, accurate, and active so it shows up more often in Google Maps and local search, and so the people who find it have a reason to call, visit, or book.

The name changed, but most business owners still say "GMB," so you'll see both terms used. This guide explains what the work actually involves, what Google says affects local visibility, and what you can do yourself before you decide whether to hire help.

What is GMB optimization, in plain English?

Your Business Profile is the box that appears on the right side of Google results, or in the list under the map, when someone searches for a business like yours. It holds your name, address, phone number, hours, photos, reviews, and a short description.

Optimizing it means three things:

  • Accuracy: every detail matches the real world and your website.
  • Completeness: every section that applies to your business is filled in, not left blank.
  • Activity: you keep it current with fresh photos, updates, and replies to reviews.

None of this involves tricks. Google states plainly in its own help center that there's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. What you can control is how clearly your profile describes your business and how well it matches what people search for.

How does Google decide which profiles to show?

Google's help page on how to improve your local ranking names three main factors:

  • Relevance: how well your profile matches what someone searched for. Complete, detailed information helps Google understand what you do.
  • Distance: how far your business is from the person searching, or from the location they named in the search.
  • Prominence: how well known your business is. Google points to things like links from other websites and the number of reviews you have.

You can't move your building closer to every customer, so most optimization work goes into relevance and prominence. That's where accurate categories, a full profile, steady reviews, and consistent listings across the web make a difference.

What does GMB optimization include?

A thorough optimization usually covers the following areas. If you're doing it yourself, treat this as a checklist.

  1. Claim and verify the profile. Verification shows Google you're authorized to manage the business. Until it's verified, your edits may not show and you have less control over the listing.
  2. Use your real business name. Enter the name customers see on your sign, website, and paperwork. Adding keywords or city names to the name breaks Google's rules and can get the profile suspended.
  3. Choose the right primary category. This is one of the most important fields. Pick the most specific category that describes what your business is, then add only a few secondary categories that also fit.
  4. Set your address or service area correctly. If customers come to you, show your address. If you travel to customers and don't serve them at your location, hide the address and set a service area instead.
  5. Keep hours current. Add regular hours and special hours for holidays or closures so people don't show up to a locked door.
  6. Write a clear description. Explain what you do, who you serve, and where, in natural language. Skip links, sales claims, and keyword lists.
  7. List your services or products. These fields help Google match you to more specific searches and help customers see what you offer before they click.
  8. Add attributes. Details like accessibility features, parking, or online appointments answer common questions at a glance.
  9. Upload real photos. Show your exterior, interior, team, and work. Real photos help people recognize you and trust what they're seeing.
  10. Link to the right page. Send the website button to the page that best matches the profile, often your homepage or a location page.

What should you avoid?

Google's guidelines for representing your business spell out what isn't allowed. The mistakes I see most often in profile audits:

  • Stuffing keywords, locations, or taglines into the business name.
  • Selecting a long list of categories "just in case." Google asks you to use as few as possible to describe your core business.
  • Showing a home address when you're a service-area business that doesn't meet customers there.
  • Creating extra profiles for the same business to cover more neighborhoods or services.
  • Letting your hours, phone number, or address drift out of sync with your website and other directories.

Breaking these rules can lead to a suspended profile, which is much harder to fix than to prevent.

Why do reviews and listings matter so much?

Reviews feed directly into prominence, and they're often the first thing a customer reads. Ask happy customers for reviews as part of your normal process, and reply to them, positive and negative. Google notes that replying shows customers you value their feedback. Never offer incentives for reviews or post reviews on your own behalf.

Your profile also doesn't exist in isolation. Google compares what it sees on your profile with what it finds on your website and other sites that list your business. If your name, address, and phone number are inconsistent across directories, that creates doubt. Cleaning up those listings is the job of local citation management, and building a steady flow of feedback is the job of online review management.

How do you know it's working?

Inside your Business Profile, the Performance section shows how people found you and what they did next, such as calls, direction requests, and website clicks. Track those numbers month over month rather than day to day, since local search results move around.

A few habits help:

  • Add UTM tags (short labels at the end of a URL that tell analytics where a click came from) to your website link so visits from your profile show up separately in GA4.
  • Note when you make big changes, like a new primary category, so you can compare before and after.
  • Search for your main services from a few locations you serve to see where you appear, keeping in mind that results vary by the searcher's location.

Is GMB the same as Google Business Profile?

Yes. GMB is the old name for Google Business Profile, and you now manage it directly from Google Search and Google Maps or through the Business Profile Manager. The listing, the reviews, and the data are the same. People still search for "GMB optimization" out of habit, so the two terms usually mean the same work: improving how your business appears and performs in local results.

How long does GMB optimization take to show results?

It depends on where you're starting and how competitive your area is. Fixing a wrong category or missing hours can change what searches you show up for fairly quickly, while building reviews and consistent listings is gradual. Plan to measure over a few months, not a few days. Anyone who guarantees a specific ranking or timeline is promising something Google itself says can't be bought.

Can you optimize your profile yourself?

Yes. Everything in the checklist above can be done by a business owner with access to the profile. Where outside help tends to pay off is in choosing categories, cleaning up inconsistent listings across many directories, recovering suspended profiles, and keeping up with posts, photos, and review replies when you don't have time. Start with the basics and decide from there.

Do you need a website to have a Business Profile?

No, you can create and verify a profile without one. But a website gives Google more information to confirm what you do and where you do it, and it gives customers somewhere to go after they find you. A simple, accurate site with your name, address, phone number, and services on it makes your profile stronger.

title: Google Business Profile Optimization for Architects: A Practical Checklist
seo_title: GMB Optimization Services for Architects: Checklist
meta_description: A practical checklist for GMB optimization services for architects: categories, practitioner profiles, service areas, project photos, and reviews.
excerpt: Architecture firms have quirks generic local SEO advice misses. This checklist covers how to set up a Google Business Profile that fits how clients actually find an architect.
tags: Google Business Profile, architects, local SEO, GMB, reviews
topic: Google Business Profile setup checklist tailored to architecture firms and solo architects
reason: Industry-specific commercial-intent post supporting the GMB optimization service page for architecture firms
body_html:
Good GMB optimization services for architects set up your Google Business Profile to match how clients actually look for a firm: the right category, a clear service area, real project photos, and steady reviews from finished projects. This checklist walks through each piece so you can do it yourself or judge someone else's work.

Architecture firms have a few quirks that generic local SEO advice misses. Projects run for months or years, clients often meet you on site instead of at your office, and many firms are one or two licensed architects rather than a storefront. Each of those affects how your profile should be set up.

Why does a Business Profile matter for an architecture firm?

When someone searches for an architect near them, Google usually shows a map with a short list of firms before the regular results. Those listings come from Business Profiles. For many prospective clients, that list is the first shortlist they make.

Google says its local results are based mainly on relevance, distance, and prominence, as explained on its page about how to improve your local ranking. For an architect, that translates to: describe your practice accurately, set your location honestly, and build a track record of reviews and mentions. Google also states that you can't pay for a better local ranking, so the work is about clarity and consistency, not shortcuts.

What should GMB optimization services for architects cover?

Whether you hire help or do it in-house, a complete setup for an architecture practice includes the items below.

1. Decide who gets a profile

Google's guidelines for representing your business have rules for "individual practitioners," public-facing professionals such as doctors, lawyers, and real estate agents. Architects aren't named in that list, but the same rules are a sensible guide for a firm. In practice, that means:

  • A firm with an office should have one profile for that location, named the way it appears on your door and letterhead.
  • A principal who meets clients directly at that office during posted hours may qualify for a separate practitioner profile, named only with their own name.
  • Support staff shouldn't have their own profiles, and one person shouldn't have several profiles for different specialties.

If you're a solo architect, keep it simple: one profile for your practice. For a single practitioner at a branded firm, Google suggests sharing one profile with the firm, named in the format "Firm Name: Your Name."

2. Use your real firm name

Enter the name clients see on your signage, website, and contracts. Don't add "Residential Architect Albany" or similar keywords to the name. Google doesn't allow it, and it can lead to a suspended profile.

3. Pick a specific primary category

Choose the most specific category that describes what your firm is, such as Architect. Add a secondary category only if it describes another real part of the business, like a landscape practice you actually run. Google asks you to use as few categories as possible and not to use categories as keywords.

4. Set your address or service area honestly

If clients can visit your studio during business hours, show your address. If you work from home and always meet clients on site, hide the address and set a service area instead. Google's guidelines say a service area generally shouldn't extend beyond about two hours of driving time from your base.

5. List your services in plain language

Use the services section to spell out what you do, for example new home design, additions and renovations, commercial interiors, adaptive reuse, feasibility studies, or permit drawings. Use the words clients use, not only industry terms.

6. Write a description that sounds like you

In a few short paragraphs, explain the kinds of projects you take on, who you work with, and the area you serve. Mention licenses or professional memberships only if they're current and accurate. Leave out links and promotional claims.

7. Show your work with real photos

Photos are where an architecture firm can stand out. Add finished interiors and exteriors, a few process shots like site visits or models, and a photo of your team or studio. Make sure you have the rights to use professional project photography, and label renderings so nobody mistakes a concept for a completed building.

8. Point the website button at the right page

Link to the page that best matches the profile, usually your homepage or a page for that office. If you have more than one office, give each location its own page with its own address and projects. My location page optimization work focuses on exactly this.

How do architects get more Google reviews?

Architecture is a low-volume, high-value business. You may finish a handful of projects a year, so you won't build reviews the way a coffee shop does. That makes each one count.

  • Ask at a natural milestone: project completion, move-in, or the final walkthrough.
  • Make it easy: send the direct review link from your profile in a short, personal email.
  • Ask past clients too: people who were happy with a project a year or two ago can still leave a review.
  • Reply to every review: thank people by name and mention the project type when it's appropriate. Google notes that replying shows you value feedback.
  • Stay within the rules: no gifts or discounts for reviews, and no reviews from staff or family.

If keeping up with requests and replies keeps slipping, a review management routine can help keep it consistent.

A quick checklist for your firm's profile

  1. Profile is claimed and verified.
  2. Business name matches your signage and website exactly.
  3. Primary category is specific and accurate; secondary categories are few and real.
  4. Address shown only if clients visit; otherwise a service area is set.
  5. Regular hours and holiday hours are current.
  6. Services list covers your main project types.
  7. Description explains what you do, for whom, and where.
  8. A solid set of real, current project and team photos is uploaded.
  9. Website link goes to the matching page, with a UTM tag (a short label on the URL) so GA4 can show visits from your profile.
  10. A review request is part of your project close-out process.
  11. Name, address, and phone match across your website and professional directories.

Do architects need a separate profile for each office?

Yes, if each office is a real, staffed location where clients can meet you during posted hours. Each one gets its own profile, its own verified address, and ideally its own page on your website. A virtual office or a mailing address with no staff doesn't qualify, and creating profiles for places you don't operate risks suspension of the whole account.

Should architects post updates on their Business Profile?

It's worth doing if you can keep it up. Short updates about completed projects, open houses, or talks you're giving keep the profile current and give prospective clients something new to look at. Once or twice a month is plenty. A profile full of old posts can look abandoned, so pick a pace you can sustain.

What should you ask before hiring GMB optimization services?

Ask what they'll change, why, and how they'll report on it. Good answers mention categories, services, photos, reviews, and listing consistency. Be cautious of anyone who promises a specific map ranking, wants to add keywords to your business name, or suggests creating extra profiles for nearby towns. Those tactics break Google's rules and put your profile at risk.

title: SEO Report Template: What to Include in a Monthly Client Report
seo_title: SEO Report Template: What to Include Each Month
meta_description: Use this SEO report template to build a clear monthly client report: summary, leads, Search Console data, keywords, technical health, and next steps.
excerpt: A simple monthly SEO report template that leads with business results, then backs them up with visibility, keyword, and technical data.
tags: seo reporting, client reports, search console, ga4, data studio
topic: Section-by-section template for a monthly SEO client report
reason: Supports the SEO reporting service page with a practical template people search for
body_html:
A good SEO report template covers six things every month: a short summary, organic traffic and leads, search visibility from Search Console, keyword movement, technical health, and the work done plus what comes next. Keep it to a few pages and lead with outcomes, not raw charts.

Most monthly reports fail for the same reason. They show everything the tools can export, and the client still can't answer the one question they care about: is this working? The template below is built around that question. Use it as a checklist for your own reports, whether you send a PDF, a slide deck, or a live dashboard.

What should an SEO report template include?

Here is the structure, in the order a client should read it. Each section answers a different question, so nothing overlaps.

  1. Executive summary. Three to five sentences: what changed, why, and what you're doing about it.
  2. Business results. Organic sessions, leads, calls, or sales from organic search.
  3. Search visibility. Clicks, impressions, click-through rate, and average position from Google Search Console.
  4. Keyword movement. How your priority keywords moved, grouped by topic or service.
  5. Technical health. Indexing issues, Core Web Vitals, and anything that broke.
  6. Work completed and next steps. What you shipped this month and what's planned for next month.

If a client only reads one page, it should be the first one. Everything after it is supporting evidence.

Section by section: how to fill in the template

1. Executive summary

Write this last, after you've looked at the data. Say what happened in plain words, compare it to last month and the same month last year, and name the likely reason. Seasonal businesses especially need the year-over-year view, or a normal slow month looks like a problem.

A useful summary sounds like this: "Organic leads were up compared with last month, mostly from the new service pages. Clicks dipped on the blog because two older posts lost positions. We're refreshing both this month." No jargon, no hedging, one clear next step.

2. Business results

This is the section clients care about most, so put it before the SEO metrics. Pull organic sessions and key events from GA4. Key events are the actions you've marked as important in Google Analytics, such as form submissions, calls, or purchases. Google's help page on key events in Google Analytics explains how any event you collect can be marked as one.

If key events aren't set up yet, fix that before you build the report. Without them, you can only report traffic, and traffic alone doesn't tell a business owner whether SEO is paying off.

3. Search visibility

Google Search Console shows how your site performs in Google Search itself, before anyone reaches the site. The Search Console Performance report gives you four core metrics:

  • Clicks: how often people clicked through to your site.
  • Impressions: how often your site appeared in results.
  • CTR (click-through rate): clicks divided by impressions.
  • Average position: the average position of your site's topmost result.

Show the trend, not just the monthly total. Rising impressions with flat clicks often means you're showing up for more searches but in lower positions, which is usually a good early sign. Falling impressions is the one to dig into.

4. Keyword movement

Don't paste a list of 300 keywords. Pick the 10 to 30 that match the client's services and group them, for example "emergency plumbing" or "kitchen remodeling." Report how each group moved and call out any big wins or drops.

Rankings come from a rank tracker such as Semrush, Ahrefs, or a similar tool, or from query data in Search Console. Note which source you use, because the numbers won't match exactly. If you'd rather hand this part off, keyword tracking and rank reporting can run on its own schedule.

5. Technical health

Keep this short unless something is wrong. Check the Pages report in Search Console for new indexing problems, and the Core Web Vitals report, which groups pages as Good, Needs improvement, or Poor based on real visitor data. The three metrics are LCP (how fast the main content loads), INP (how quickly the page responds to taps and clicks), and CLS (how much the layout jumps around).

A one-line status per item is enough: "No new indexing issues. Mobile Core Web Vitals: all URLs Good." Expand only when there's a problem and a fix to explain.

6. Work completed and next steps

List what you actually did: pages optimized, posts published, links earned, fixes shipped. Then list the plan for next month. This section connects your effort to the results above it, and it's often the part clients remember.

How long should a monthly SEO report be?

Short enough to read in five minutes. For most small and mid-size businesses, that means a one-page summary followed by two to four pages of supporting charts. If a chart doesn't change a decision or explain a result, leave it out or move it to an appendix.

What tools can you use to build the template?

You don't need a paid reporting platform to start. Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio), Google's free dashboard tool, connects directly to Search Console and GA4, so the numbers update on their own. It can also email a PDF of the report on a schedule, which means clients get the report on the same day every month.

Slide decks and spreadsheets work too, especially when you add written commentary. The format matters less than consistency: same sections, same order, same date ranges, every month.

SEO report template mistakes to avoid

  • Leading with rankings. Rankings are a means, not the result. Put leads and sales first.
  • Changing metrics month to month. If the template keeps shifting, clients can't compare progress.
  • No context. A number without a comparison period or an explanation is just a number.
  • Hiding bad months. Name the drop, explain the likely cause, and show the plan. Clients trust reports that are honest about dips.
  • Too many vanity metrics. Total backlinks or domain scores rarely help a business owner make a decision.

Frequently asked questions

How often should you send an SEO report?

Monthly works for most businesses. SEO changes slowly, so weekly reports tend to show noise rather than progress, and clients start reacting to normal swings. A monthly report with a quarterly review, where you step back and look at three months of trends together, gives enough rhythm to stay accountable without overreacting. Send it on the same day each month so it becomes routine.

Should an SEO report show keyword rankings?

Yes, but as supporting detail, not the headline. Group priority keywords by service or topic and show how each group moved. A single keyword's position can change daily based on location, device, and personalization, so focus on trends across groups. Pair rankings with clicks and leads so the client can see whether better positions are actually bringing in business.

What's the difference between an SEO report and an SEO audit?

A report tracks ongoing performance month to month: traffic, visibility, rankings, and the work completed. An audit is a one-time, deep review of a site to find problems and opportunities, such as technical errors, content gaps, or weak pages. The audit usually sets the plan, and the monthly report shows whether that plan is working. Many businesses get an audit first, then move to monthly reporting.

Can you automate an SEO report?

You can automate the data, not the thinking. Dashboard tools like Data Studio pull fresh numbers from Search Console and GA4 automatically and can email the report on a schedule. What still needs a person is the summary: explaining why numbers moved and what you'll do about it. That written context is what makes a report useful rather than just a set of charts.

title: How to Track Keyword Revenue: Connecting Rankings to Sales
seo_title: Keyword Revenue Tracking: Connect Rankings to Sales
meta_description: Keyword revenue tracking, step by step: join GA4 landing page revenue with Search Console query data to see which keywords bring in sales and leads.
excerpt: GA4 won't show revenue by organic keyword, but you can estimate it by joining landing page revenue with Search Console query data. Here's how.
tags: keyword tracking, ga4, search console, seo roi, revenue attribution
topic: Estimating revenue per organic keyword by joining GA4 and Search Console on landing page
reason: Supports the keyword tracking service page by showing how rankings tie back to revenue
body_html:
Keyword revenue tracking links the searches people use to find you with the sales or leads those visits bring in. Google Analytics doesn't report organic keywords next to revenue, so you connect them through landing pages: keywords lead to pages, and pages lead to revenue.

The result is an estimate, not an exact receipt for every keyword. But it's a far better guide than rankings alone, because it shows which searches are actually worth your time and which ones only bring traffic.

Why can't you see revenue by keyword in GA4?

Google doesn't pass the search term to your site when someone clicks an organic result, so Google Analytics never sees it. Search Console does have query data, and you can link it to GA4. But Google's help page on the GA4 Queries report notes that query data can be broken down by Search Console dimensions, such as country and device, but not by Analytics dimensions. In practice, that means you can't line a query up against the sales or key events it led to.

So there's no single report that says "this keyword made this much money." You have to build the connection yourself, and the landing page is the bridge.

How keyword revenue tracking works

The method has three parts:

  1. Revenue by landing page from GA4, filtered to organic search.
  2. Clicks by keyword and landing page from Search Console.
  3. A join on the landing page URL, which splits each page's revenue across the keywords that sent clicks to it.

If a page earned a set amount of revenue from organic visits, and one keyword brought 60% of that page's clicks, you credit that keyword with roughly 60% of the page's revenue. It assumes every click to a page is equally likely to convert, which isn't strictly true. It's still close enough to compare keywords and set priorities.

Step 1: Make sure revenue is being measured

Everything depends on GA4 recording value. For online stores, that means the GA4 ecommerce purchase event, sent with a value and a currency.

For service businesses without online checkout, mark your lead actions (form submissions, calls, booking requests) as key events and give them a value. Google Analytics lets you set a default key event value that applies whenever the event doesn't send its own. A reasonable starting point: your average job value multiplied by your close rate. If an average job brings in $2,000 and you close one in four leads, each lead is worth about $500 to you.

Note that a default value only applies to future events, so start this as early as you can.

Step 2: Pull organic revenue by landing page

In GA4, open the Landing page report, which shows key events and total revenue for each page where a visit started. Filter or add a comparison so you only see organic search traffic, for example by session default channel group or by session source / medium equal to google / organic.

Export the landing page, organic sessions, key events, and revenue for the date range you're reviewing. Total revenue only counts purchases, subscriptions, and ad revenue, so for a lead-based business it will usually show zero. In that case, multiply each page's organic key events by the lead value you worked out in Step 1. Three months is a good minimum, because single months are often too small to be reliable.

Step 3: Pull keyword clicks by page from Search Console

In Search Console's Performance report, use the same date range and export queries with their pages. The web interface limits how many rows you can export, so for larger sites use the Search Console connector in Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio), the Search Console API, or the bulk data export to BigQuery.

Some queries are hidden by Google for privacy, so the query clicks for a page won't always add up to its total clicks. That's normal. Base your percentages on the clicks you can see.

Step 4: Join the data and assign revenue

In a spreadsheet or Data Studio, match the two exports on landing page URL. Clean the URLs first so they match: same protocol, same trailing slash, no tracking parameters. Then for each keyword:

  • Divide the keyword's clicks to that page by the page's total visible clicks.
  • Multiply that share by the page's organic revenue.
  • Add up across pages if a keyword sends clicks to more than one URL.

Now you have an estimated revenue figure per keyword. Sort by it, and you'll often find that the keywords bringing the most traffic aren't the ones bringing the most money.

Step 5: Use it to make decisions

The point of keyword revenue tracking is to change what you work on next. A few ways to use it:

  • Protect your earners. Watch the rankings of your highest-revenue keywords closely and refresh those pages first if they slip.
  • Push near-misses. Keywords ranking in positions 5 to 15 with strong revenue per click are often the best return on new effort.
  • Rethink traffic-only content. Pages with lots of clicks and little revenue may need a clearer next step, a better offer, or a different target keyword.
  • Guide new content. Use the patterns you see to choose topics during keyword research.

Frequently asked questions

Is keyword revenue tracking accurate?

It's an informed estimate. Splitting a page's revenue by click share assumes all clicks to that page convert at the same rate, and some queries are hidden in Search Console. It also only counts revenue from the session where the visit started on that page, so longer buying journeys get under-credited. Treat the numbers as a way to rank keywords against each other, not as exact dollar amounts for a financial report.

Can you track revenue by keyword for Google Ads?

Yes, and it's much more direct. Paid search platforms record which keyword triggered each ad click, so conversions and conversion values can be reported by keyword inside the ad account. The landing page method in this guide is mainly for organic search, where the search term isn't passed to your analytics. If you run both, keep the two reports separate so you don't double count.

How often should you review keyword revenue data?

Quarterly works well for most businesses. Monthly data is often too thin, especially for service businesses with a modest number of leads, and small samples make the numbers swing. Look at a rolling three to six months, compare against the previous period, and adjust your priorities from there. Check rankings for your top revenue keywords more often so you catch drops early.

title: White Label Reporting for Agencies: What to Show Clients and How to Brand It
seo_title: White Label Reporting for Agencies: What to Show
meta_description: A guide to white label reporting for agencies: what to include in client reports, how to brand them, and how to manage data access with partners.
excerpt: What agencies should put in white label client reports, how to brand them properly, and how to keep data access clean when a partner does the work.

topic: What agencies should include in white-labeled client reports and how to brand and deliver them
reason: Supports the custom reporting dashboards white label page for agencies evaluating reporting partners
body_html:
White label reporting means delivering client reports under your agency's brand, even when a partner does the work or builds the dashboards. Done well, it shows clients a clear story: results first, then visibility, rankings, and the work completed, all in your logo, colors, and voice.

If you resell SEO, PPC, or social services, the report is often the only part of the work your client actually sees each month. It carries your reputation. This guide covers what to include, how to brand it, how to handle data access, and the mistakes that make white label reports feel generic.

What is white label reporting?

In a white label arrangement, a partner agency or freelancer handles part of the delivery, and you present it as your own. White label reporting extends that to the reports: the dashboards, PDFs, or decks your client receives carry only your branding. There's no partner logo, no unfamiliar email address, and no tool watermarks that point somewhere else.

That doesn't mean hiding the truth about results. The numbers come straight from the client's own accounts, such as Google Search Console, GA4, or Google Ads. Only the presentation is yours.

What should a white label report show clients?

Clients don't want more data. They want to know whether the money they spend with you is working. Build every report around that, in this order:

  1. A short written summary. What changed this period, why, and what's next. Three to five sentences in plain language.
  2. Business outcomes. Leads, calls, bookings, or sales from the channels you manage. In GA4, these are the actions marked as key events.
  3. Channel performance. For SEO: clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position from Search Console. For paid search: spend, conversions, and cost per conversion. For social: reach and engagement tied to clicks or leads.
  4. Priority keywords or campaigns. A focused set, grouped by service or theme, with movement since last period.
  5. Health checks. Indexing issues, Core Web Vitals, broken tracking, or ad disapprovals. One line each unless something needs attention.
  6. Work completed and next steps. What was delivered and what's planned. This is where the partner's work becomes visible to the client, under your name.

Keep comparisons consistent. Show the current period against the previous period and, for seasonal businesses, the same period last year. Without that context, a normal seasonal dip reads like a failure.

What to leave out

  • Tool-specific scores that clients can't act on, unless you explain them.
  • Raw keyword dumps of hundreds of rows. Move them to an appendix if a client asks for them.
  • Internal notes meant for your partner, like task IDs or production comments.
  • Metrics that change every month. Pick a set and stick with it, so clients can compare progress over time.

How to brand a white label report

Branding is more than swapping a logo. A client should feel the report came from the same team they talk to on calls.

Visual branding

Use your logo, brand colors, and fonts across every page. If you build reports in Data Studio, Google's free dashboard tool (called Looker Studio until its rename back to Data Studio in April 2026), you can set a report theme for colors and fonts. Its theme settings can even generate a color palette from an image, so text and chart colors can match your logo. Custom themes don't carry from one report to the next, so build one branded template and copy it for each client.

Delivery branding

The report should arrive from you. That means:

  • Emails sent from your domain or your team's addresses, not a partner's.
  • Shared dashboards owned by an account your agency controls.
  • File names, page titles, and footers that use your agency name.
  • Your contact details on the report, so questions come to you.

Data Studio can email a PDF of the report on a schedule, with a link back to the live version. Set the schedule from an account your agency owns so the delivery comes from you. The free edition allows one schedule per report and a daily maximum frequency; the Pro edition raises those limits.

Voice branding

The written summary is where most white label reports give themselves away. Generic text that reads the same for every client tells them nobody looked closely. Write the summary in your agency's voice, mention the client's own goals, and connect the numbers to decisions you've discussed with them. If your partner drafts it, edit it before it goes out.

How should agencies handle data access for white label reporting?

Access is where white label setups often get messy. A few rules keep it clean and safe.

The client should own their accounts. Search Console, GA4, Google Business Profile, and ad accounts belong to the client's business. Your agency gets access, and your partner gets access through you. If the relationship ends, the client keeps their data.

Give partners the least access they need. Search Console has three permission levels: owner, full user, and restricted user. According to Google's help page on managing Search Console owners, users, and permissions, restricted users can view most data but can't take actions like submitting sitemaps. For reporting alone, that's often enough. Apply the same thinking in GA4 and ad platforms.

Keep a simple access log. List which accounts each client has, who has access, and at what level. Review it when a partner or employee changes.

Which tools work for white label reporting?

You can start with free tools and add paid ones as your client list grows. Common options include:

  • Data Studio: connects directly to Search Console, GA4, and Google Ads, with custom themes and scheduled email delivery.
  • SEO platforms: tools like Semrush and Ahrefs include rank tracking and report builders with options for adding your own branding, depending on the plan.
  • Slides or documents: useful for quarterly reviews, where commentary matters more than live data.

Whatever you choose, aim for one consistent template across clients. It's faster to produce, easier to check, and makes onboarding a new client a matter of connecting data sources rather than designing from scratch. If you'd rather not build and maintain that template yourself, custom white label reporting dashboards can be set up under your brand.

Common white label reporting mistakes

  • Leaving traces of the partner. A stray logo, an unfamiliar sender, or a dashboard URL owned by someone else raises questions you don't want to answer mid-campaign.
  • Reporting activity instead of results. "We published four posts" matters less than what those posts did for leads.
  • Skipping quality checks. Broken charts or date ranges that don't match make your agency look careless, even if the partner made the error. Review every report before it goes out.
  • Hiding bad months. Explain drops honestly, with a likely cause and a plan. Clients forgive dips far more readily than surprises.
  • Overpromising in the summary. Never imply guaranteed rankings or traffic. Report what happened and what you're doing next.

Frequently asked questions

Is white label reporting honest?

Yes, as long as the data is real and unedited. White labeling changes who presents the work, not what the work achieved. Your agency is still responsible for the results, the strategy, and the client relationship. The numbers should come directly from the client's own accounts, and the written summary should describe them accurately, including the months that don't go well. Some agencies also mention to clients that they work with specialist partners.

How often should agencies send white label reports?

Monthly reporting suits most SEO and social clients, since those channels change gradually. Paid search clients with larger budgets may want a live dashboard they can check any time, plus a monthly summary. Add a quarterly review for every client to step back and look at trends together. Whatever schedule you choose, keep it consistent so the report becomes a dependable part of your service.

Who should write the summary in a white label report?

Whoever writes the first draft, someone at your agency should finish it. Your partner may know the data best, but you know the client: their goals, worries, and what you promised on the last call. Have the partner send a draft with key findings, then edit it into your own voice and add client-specific context. That final pass is what makes the report feel personal rather than templated.

Can clients see where the report data comes from?

They should be able to. Showing data sources, such as Search Console, GA4, or Google Ads, builds trust because clients can check the numbers in their own accounts. White label reporting removes the partner's branding, not the source of the data. Label each section with its source and date range, and give clients access to their own accounts so they never depend on you just to see their numbers.

Your clients see your name, and you get a partner who reports results plainly.

title: White Label Consultants: When Agencies Should Bring One In

excerpt: White label consultants let your agency add specialist skill without adding headcount. Here's how to tell when it's time, and how to set it up so your clients stay yours.

topic: When and how agencies should bring in white label consultants for SEO and marketing work
reason: Supports the SEO outsourcing page by targeting agencies weighing outside specialist help.
body_html:
White label consultants are outside specialists who work behind your agency's brand, so your clients see your team and your name while the consultant handles strategy, audits or execution. Agencies usually bring one in when demand outruns in-house skill, capacity or time.

That definition is simple. Deciding when it makes sense is harder. Bring someone in too early and you add a layer you don't need. Wait too long and deadlines slip, quality drops and your best people burn out. This post walks through the signals worth watching, what a good arrangement looks like, and how to protect your client relationships while you do it.

What do white label consultants actually do?

A white label consultant is different from a general freelancer you hand tasks to. The consultant brings judgment, not just hours. Depending on the arrangement, that can include:

  • Strategy: building an SEO roadmap, a content plan or a local search plan your account team presents.
  • Audits: technical, content or backlink reviews delivered in your branded template.
  • Execution: on-page changes, content briefs, Google Business Profile work or reporting, done inside your systems.
  • Second opinions: reviewing a struggling account and telling you plainly what's wrong.

The "white label" part means the work goes out under your brand. Your client talks to your account lead. The consultant may join calls as a member of your team, or may never speak to the client at all. You decide which.

When should agencies bring in white label consultants?

There's no single trigger, but a few patterns show up again and again. If two or more of these sound familiar, it's worth a conversation.

You're turning down work you could sell

If a client asks for SEO alongside their paid search or web build, and you say no because nobody on staff can do it well, you're handing that budget to someone else. A consultant lets you say yes without hiring before the revenue is steady.

One person holds all the specialist knowledge

Many agencies have a single SEO lead. When that person is out, on leave or overloaded, everything stalls. A consultant gives you a second set of hands who already knows how you work.

Demand is real but uneven

Maybe you get three technical audits one month and none the next. A full-time hire for uneven work is a hard call. A consultant scales up and down with your pipeline.

Client results have flattened

Sometimes the issue isn't capacity. It's that the team has been running the same playbook for years. A fresh, senior set of eyes on a few accounts can surface problems that are easy to miss from the inside, such as crawl and indexing issues, thin location pages or reporting that tracks activity instead of outcomes.

You're adding a new service line

Launching AI search visibility, local SEO or reporting dashboards as a new offer? A consultant can help you build the process, templates and pricing logic while you find out whether the market wants it.

When is a white label consultant the wrong fit?

Outside help isn't always the answer. It's probably not the right move if:

  • You don't yet know what you'd hand off. A consultant needs a defined scope, not "help with SEO."
  • Your core problem is sales or client management, not delivery.
  • The work is steady and full time. At that point, a hire may serve you better long term.
  • You can't give the consultant access to the tools and data they need to do the job properly.

What to look for before you sign anything

Google's own guidance on hiring an SEO is a good starting checklist, and it applies just as well when the client is your agency. It suggests asking for examples of past work, asking whether the person follows Google Search Essentials, asking how success will be measured, and asking whether they'll explain every change they make. It also warns that no one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google.

On top of that, check for agency-specific fit:

  1. Brand discipline. Will they work in your templates, your tone and your tools without adding their own logo or contact details?
  2. Clear scope and turnaround. Ask for written deliverables and timelines before the first project.
  3. Communication rhythm. Agree on how updates arrive, who answers client questions and how fast.
  4. Confidentiality. Put non-solicitation and confidentiality terms in writing so client relationships stay yours.
  5. Transparency with you. Even if the client never sees the consultant, you should see everything: what changed, why and what happened next.

How to set up access without losing control

Give consultants the access they need and nothing more. For Search Console, Google offers owner, full and restricted user levels. According to Google's help page on managing Search Console owners, users and permissions, full users can view all data and take some actions, such as submitting sitemaps, while restricted users have mostly view-only access. For an audit, restricted access is often enough.

A few habits help:

  • Keep the client or your agency as the owner of every account. Add the consultant as a user.
  • Use named logins instead of shared passwords so you know who did what.
  • Write down every account the consultant can reach, and remove access when the project ends.

How to start small

The lowest-risk way to test a partnership is one defined project with a clear finish line. A technical audit, a content brief set for one client or a month of reporting all work well. Judge the result on accuracy, how well it matched your brand and how much editing your team had to do before it went out.

If that goes well, move to a recurring scope. The post on scaling your agency with white label partners covers how to grow from a single project into an ongoing arrangement, and white label project management can keep multi-client work on schedule.

Are white label consultants the same as freelancers?

Not quite. A freelancer is often hired to complete defined tasks, like writing articles or building pages. White label consultants usually bring strategy and judgment as well as execution, and they deliver under your agency's brand. Some freelancers work this way too, so the label matters less than the arrangement: who sets direction, whose brand goes on the work and who owns the client relationship.

Will my clients know I'm using a consultant?

Only if you tell them. In a white label setup, deliverables go out in your branded templates and your account lead stays the main contact. Some agencies choose to introduce the consultant as part of their team for calls. Whatever you decide, be consistent, and make sure your contracts with clients allow you to use subcontractors.

How do I keep a consultant from going around me to my clients?

Put it in writing. A clear agreement with confidentiality and non-solicitation terms sets expectations from the start. Beyond the paperwork, keep ownership of every account with your agency or client, route client communication through your team and work with people who have a track record of agency partnerships. A good partner has no interest in competing with the agencies that send them work.

What should I hand off first?

Start with something self-contained and easy to judge. Technical SEO audits, keyword research and monthly reporting are common first projects because they have a clear deliverable and a clear deadline. Avoid starting with your most sensitive account. Once you've seen how the consultant works with your templates and timelines, expand into ongoing strategy or execution.

Add SEO capacity without adding headcount

title: How to Outsource SEO Projects: Scoping, QA and Handoff
seo_title: Outsourcing SEO Projects: Scoping, QA and Handoff
meta_description: A practical guide to outsourcing SEO projects: how to write the scope, what access to give, QA checklists, and what a clean handoff should include.
excerpt: Outsourced SEO goes smoothly when you scope it in writing, check the work before it ships and hand off access and files cleanly. Here's a checklist for each stage.
tags: SEO outsourcing, project scoping, quality assurance, agency operations, white label
topic: A step-by-step process for scoping, quality-checking and handing off outsourced SEO projects
reason: Supports the SEO outsourcing page with a practical how-to for agencies and marketers handing off SEO work.
body_html:
Outsourcing SEO projects works best when you treat it as three jobs: scoping the work in writing, checking quality before anything reaches a client or a live site, and handing off access, files and results cleanly at the end. Skip any one and the project gets harder to manage.

Whether you're an agency sending work to a white label partner or an in-house marketer hiring outside help, the risks are the same. Vague briefs lead to the wrong deliverable. Unchecked changes reach a live site. And when the project ends, nobody is sure who owns what. Here's a practical process for each stage.

How do you scope an outsourced SEO project?

A good scope answers one question: what does "done" look like? If you can't describe the finished deliverable, the person doing the work can't either.

Write a short brief that covers:

  • The goal. One or two sentences on the business outcome, such as more qualified leads from service pages or fixing pages that dropped out of the index.
  • The deliverable. An audit document, a set of content briefs, implemented on-page changes, a reporting dashboard. Be specific about format.
  • In scope and out of scope. List what's included and, just as important, what isn't. "Technical audit of the main site, not the blog subdomain" saves a lot of back and forth.
  • Inputs you'll provide. Brand guidelines, target keywords, past audits, competitor lists, client notes.
  • Access needed. Which tools, at what level, and who grants it.
  • Timeline and checkpoints. A due date plus at least one mid-project check-in.
  • Revision rounds. How many, and what counts as a revision versus new work.

If you're an agency, add your white label rules: which template to use, whose name goes on the document and whether the partner ever talks to the client.

Match the scope to the type of project

Different SEO projects need different scoping detail. An audit needs clear boundaries, such as which domains, how many URLs and which issues to prioritize. Content work needs search intent, audience and word ranges. Implementation work needs to say who has publishing rights and whether changes go to a staging site first.

What access should you give an outside SEO?

Give the minimum access the project requires, and keep ownership in your hands or your client's. Google's guide Do you need an SEO? suggests granting only read access to Search Console during an audit, before you decide whether to give write access.

The main tools each have their own permission levels:

  • Search Console: Google's help page on managing owners, users and permissions explains that restricted users have mostly view-only access, full users can view all data and take actions like submitting sitemaps, and owners can manage other users.
  • Google Analytics 4: GA4 uses roles from Viewer up to Administrator. According to Google's page on GA4 access and data-restriction management, Viewers can see settings and data, Editors control property settings but can't manage users, and Administrators have full control.
  • Your CMS: Use an individual login with an editor-level role rather than sharing an admin password.

Keep a simple access log: tool, person, level, date granted. You'll need it at handoff.

How do you QA outsourced SEO work?

Quality assurance, or QA, is the check that happens before work goes to a client or a live site. It catches mistakes while they're still cheap to fix. Build it into the timeline from the start instead of squeezing it in at the end.

QA checklist for audits and strategy documents

  1. Spot-check a sample of flagged issues yourself. Open the URLs and confirm the problem is real.
  2. Confirm each recommendation says why it matters and what to do, not just what's wrong.
  3. Check that priorities make sense for this business, not a generic list.
  4. Look for any claim of guaranteed rankings or traffic. Google says no one can guarantee a #1 ranking, so these shouldn't appear.
  5. Make sure branding, tone and formatting match your template.

QA checklist for content

  1. Does it answer the search the keyword represents?
  2. Are facts, product names and service details correct for this client?
  3. Are internal links pointing to real, live pages?
  4. Is any outside source real and does it say what the content claims?
  5. Does it read like the client, not like a template?

QA checklist for on-site changes

  1. Review changes on a staging site first when one is available.
  2. Get a written list of every change: page, element, old value, new value.
  3. After launch, use URL Inspection in Search Console to check key pages.
  4. Watch Search Console and GA4 over the following weeks for unexpected drops in indexed pages, clicks or key events.

What should an SEO project handoff include?

Handoff is where many outsourced projects quietly fall apart. The work is done, but nobody can find the files, explain the reasoning or tell you what to watch next. A clean handoff package includes:

  • Final deliverables in editable formats, stored somewhere you own.
  • A change log listing everything that was modified on the site.
  • Open items that weren't finished or were out of scope, with a suggested owner.
  • Baseline numbers from before the project, so you can measure the effect later.
  • A short walkthrough, live or recorded, explaining the main findings and next steps.
  • Access cleanup. Remove or downgrade the partner's access in every tool on your access log, unless ongoing work has been agreed.

For Search Console, note that verified owners prove ownership with a token, such as an HTML file or DNS record. Google's permissions page explains that removing a verified owner also means removing their token, or they may be able to regain access.

Outsourcing SEO projects: common questions

These are the questions that come up most often when agencies and in-house teams start handing off SEO work.

Should I outsource SEO projects or hire in-house?

It depends on how steady the work is. Outsourcing suits defined projects, uneven demand or specialist tasks like technical audits that your team only needs occasionally. Hiring makes more sense when you have consistent, full-time work and want the knowledge to live inside your company. Many agencies do both: an in-house lead who owns strategy and an outside partner who adds capacity.

How detailed should an SEO project brief be?

Detailed enough that someone new could start without a call. That usually means the goal, the exact deliverable and its format, what's in and out of scope, inputs, access, deadlines and revision rounds. One or two pages is typical. If a brief needs ten pages, the project may be too big and could be split into phases.

How long should QA take on an outsourced SEO deliverable?

Plan for it from the start rather than guessing at the end. A simple rule is to reserve a fixed review window in the timeline, sized to the deliverable: a short content piece needs far less review than a full technical audit. What matters most is that review happens before the work reaches a client or a live site, and that someone other than the author does it.

What if the outsourced work isn't good enough?

Go back to the brief. If the deliverable missed something that was in scope, send specific feedback and use one of your agreed revision rounds. If the brief was unclear, update it and treat the fix as a lesson for next time. If quality problems keep repeating after clear feedback, that's a sign the partner isn't the right fit.

A partner for your next SEO project

If you'd rather hand off scoped SEO work to someone who follows your brief, your templates and your timeline, see how I handle SEO outsourcing for agencies. A technical SEO audit is a common first project, and I can set up custom reporting dashboards to carry results through handoff.

title: Technical SEO Audit Checklist: Crawlability, Indexing and Site Speed
seo_title: Technical SEO Audit Checklist: Crawl, Index, Speed
meta_description: Use this technical SEO audit checklist to find crawl, indexing, duplicate URL, speed, and mobile issues, and learn which fixes to tackle first.
excerpt: A practical, step-by-step technical SEO audit checklist covering crawlability, indexing, canonicals, Core Web Vitals, mobile, and structured data, plus how to prioritize fixes.

topic: A step-by-step checklist for auditing crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile, and structured data.
reason: New guide supporting the Technical SEO service page (/seo-services/technical-seo) for the keyword technical seo audit checklist.
body_html:
A technical SEO audit checklist is a step-by-step review of whether search engines can crawl, render, and index your site, and whether pages load fast enough for real visitors. Work through crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile rendering, and structured data, then fix whatever blocks the pages that matter most.

What a technical SEO audit covers

Technical SEO is the plumbing under your content. An audit answers three plain questions: can Google find your pages, can it understand and store them, and do they work well for people once they load. Great content and strong links can't help a page Google never reaches.

You don't need a big software budget to start. Google Search Console is free and shows what Google sees. A crawler such as Screaming Frog, or the site audit tools in Semrush or Ahrefs, shows what a bot finds when it follows your links. Comparing the two views is where most problems show up.

Before you start: set up your tools

  • Verify your site in Google Search Console. A domain property covers every version of the site (http, https, www, and subdomains) in one place.
  • List your most important URLs: the pages that bring in leads, sales, or calls. These get checked first and fixed first.
  • Run a full crawl of the site. If your pages rely on JavaScript to show content, turn on JavaScript rendering in your crawler.
  • Note who can change what: templates, server settings, redirects, and robots.txt often sit with different people.

Technical SEO audit checklist, part 1: crawlability

Crawlability means a search engine's bot can reach a page by following links and isn't told to stay away.

  1. Check robots.txt. Open yoursite.com/robots.txt and make sure it isn't blocking important folders, or the CSS and JavaScript files pages need to display. Remember that robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. Google's introduction to robots.txt says it is not a mechanism for keeping a page out of Google; use a noindex tag or password protection for that.
  2. Find broken internal links. Your crawler's 4xx report lists links pointing to pages that no longer exist. Update the link at the source instead of leaning on redirects forever.
  3. Clean up redirects. Look for chains (page A redirects to B, which redirects to C) and loops. Point internal links straight at the final URL and use 301 redirects for permanent moves.
  4. Look for orphan pages. These are pages no other page links to. Compare your crawl against your XML sitemap and your top landing pages in GA4 to spot them.
  5. Check click depth. Important pages should be reachable within a few clicks of the homepage. Pages buried deep in the site tend to be crawled less often.
  6. Watch for server errors. 5xx errors in your crawl, or in the Crawl Stats report under Settings in Search Console, mean your server is turning bots away.

Part 2: indexing

Indexing is Google storing a page so it can appear in search results. Open the Page indexing report in Search Console. Google says not to expect every URL on your site to be indexed, since some are duplicates or have little useful content, so focus on whether your key pages are.

  1. Review why pages aren't indexed. Sort the reasons by count. "Crawled - currently not indexed" or "Discovered - currently not indexed" on pages you care about often points to thin or duplicate content, or weak internal linking.
  2. Hunt for stray noindex tags. These often slip in during a redesign or when a "hide from search engines" setting is left on after launch.
  3. Fix soft 404s. A soft 404 is a page that says "not found" but returns a success code. Return a real 404 or 410 status for pages that are truly gone.
  4. Inspect key URLs. The URL Inspection tool shows whether a page is indexed, which canonical Google chose, and a screenshot of how Google rendered it.
  5. Audit your XML sitemap. It should list only canonical, indexable pages that return a 200 status. Google's sitemap guidelines cap each file at 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, say Google ignores the priority and changefreq fields, and say lastmod is used only when it's consistently accurate.

Part 3: duplicate URLs and canonical tags

The same content often lives at several addresses: http and https, www and non-www, with and without a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters added. A canonical is the version you want Google to treat as the main one.

  • Pick one preferred version of your domain and 301 redirect the others to it.
  • Give each indexable page a self-referencing canonical tag with an absolute URL.
  • Make sure canonicals point to live, indexable pages, not to redirects or noindexed pages.
  • Check that your sitemap, canonical tags, and internal links all name the same URL.

Google's canonicalization guide treats redirects and rel="canonical" as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weaker one. It also warns against using robots.txt or noindex to choose a canonical.

Part 4: site speed and Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals are Google's three measures of real-world page experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, loading), Interaction to Next Paint (INP, responsiveness), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS, visual stability). According to web.dev, a page passes when LCP is 2.5 seconds or less, INP is 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS is 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of visits.

  1. Start with the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console. It uses data from real Chrome users and groups similar URLs together, so one template fix can clear many pages.
  2. Run PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse on each main template (home, service, product, blog) to see what's slowing it down.
  3. Common fixes: compress and correctly size images, set width and height on images and embeds to stop layout shifts, defer JavaScript that isn't needed right away, and trim third-party scripts you no longer use.

For a deeper walkthrough, see my guide on improving site speed and Core Web Vitals.

Part 5: mobile, rendering, and HTTPS

  • Google crawls and indexes the mobile version of your site, so confirm the mobile pages carry the same main content, headings, and links as desktop.
  • If content loads with JavaScript, check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection to confirm Google sees it.
  • Serve every page over HTTPS, redirect http to https, and fix mixed content (images or scripts still loading over http).

Part 6: structured data

Structured data is code that labels what a page is about, such as a business, product, article, or FAQ, using the Schema.org vocabulary. Test key pages with Google's Rich Results Test, fix errors, and make sure the markup matches what's visible on the page.

How to prioritize what you find

An audit can surface hundreds of issues. Sort them so the work goes where it counts:

  1. Anything stopping important pages from being crawled or indexed.
  2. Site-wide template problems, since one fix repairs many pages.
  3. Speed and Core Web Vitals on your highest-traffic templates.
  4. Cleanup items, like old redirects and minor duplicate titles.

Track each issue in a spreadsheet with the affected URLs, the fix, who owns it, and the date it was fixed. Re-crawl after each round to confirm the fix held.

How often should you run a technical SEO audit?

A full audit once or twice a year works for most small and mid-size sites, with a lighter monthly check of Search Console for new indexing errors, Core Web Vitals changes, and crawl problems. Always run one before and after a redesign, platform move, or domain change, since those are the moments when redirects break, noindex tags get left behind, and pages quietly drop out of the index.

Can you do a technical SEO audit yourself?

Yes, for the basics. Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and a crawler will surface most crawl, indexing, and speed issues on a small site, and this checklist gives you the order to work in. Where it gets harder is diagnosing why a problem happens and fixing it safely, especially redirects, JavaScript rendering, and server settings. That's usually the point where a developer or SEO specialist saves time.

What's the difference between a technical SEO audit and a full SEO audit?

A technical SEO audit looks at the site's infrastructure: crawling, indexing, speed, mobile, security, and structured data. A full SEO audit adds content quality, keyword targeting, on-page optimization, backlinks, and competitors. Many people start with the technical side because content and link work only pays off once search engines can reach and index the pages you're improving.

Get help with your technical SEO
